tagline.text: A sanctuary off Matnog where big fish swim in bamboo pens

location.label: Location
location.text: Off Barangay Calintaan, Matnog, Sorsogon (Juag Island)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,600–3,000 (boat charter and registration, before splitting among the group, rough estimate)

children.text: Juag Lagoon is a privately kept fish sanctuary off Matnog in Sorsogon, maintained by one family, where you see big fish and a sea turtle up close in bamboo pens. It is a stop on the Matnog island-hopping circuit with Subic Beach and Tikling Island.

Juag Lagoon is a fish sanctuary around Juag Island off Matnog in Sorsogon. According to travel blogs and news reports it is maintained privately by the Geneblazo family, and a story is told that the owner, Alex Geneblazo, regards the fish as his children. Know before you go that it is less a government-designated marine protected area than a place one family has tended for a long time. The opening date varies by source. One guide says it began in 2000 with a few pairs of milkfish (bangus) raised on seaweed, while another report puts it about ten years before 2018. Some accounts also say it began welcoming tourists after the Matnog island-hopping circuit became known.
It is about
20 minutes

from Matnog Port by motorized outrigger boat. In the middle of the sea there are bamboo pens, and a bamboo walkway over the water and a bamboo raft pulled along ropes carry visitors to a stilted hut in the center. The pens hold a variety of large fish, about 40 species according to one source. A 2014 report gave the lagoon's area as 5,762 sq m, while another guide gives about 572 sq m, so the numbers differ widely. What matters to travelers is less the size than feeding and seeing the fish up close.

The visit is simple. At the first platform you get a safety briefing and look down on coral, water plants and fish, then cross by raft to the central hut and feed the big fish. Food is described as fish pellets, small fish and bits of bread, and one source says pellets are

/kg. Many guides say there is no entrance fee and donations are accepted. However, entering the water wearing sunscreen is prohibited, and diving is also prohibited. So snorkeling is done only in the permitted area, and otherwise you watch from the hut. A 2011 blog wrote that the owner collects marine life for research and breeding and then returns it to the sea, and a 2018 article said the fish in the pens can be touched and the raft serves as an observation deck. Such descriptions differ a little from period to period, so go by the explanation of your guide and the signs on site. Move quietly so as not to startle the fish, and feed them only the way your guide shows you.

Juag is usually one stop on the Matnog island-hopping circuit. A common course takes a single boat to Subic Beach on Calintaan Island, Tikling Island (pinkish sand) and others. Old reviews and prices are mixed together, so confirm admission rules and fees at the Matnog tourism office before you go. Read together with the Subic Beach entry, this completes a Matnog itinerary. Matnog is a first-class municipality at the southern tip of Luzon, with an area of about 162.40 sq km, 40 barangays and a 2024 population of about 42,444. One theory says its name comes from the Bicol word matonog, meaning loud sound, which recalls the sound of waves breaking on the shore. Matnog Port is one of the busiest in the region for crossing between Luzon and the Visayas, with ferries to Allen in Northern Samar. Juag, Calintaan and Murong Burongan are introduced as the three outlying islands off the port, and one tour report used the village of Poropandan as the departure point for the waters off Matnog.

blocks.title: Bamboo pens and a stilted hut

children.text: There are bamboo pens in the middle of the sea, and a bamboo raft pulled along ropes takes you to the central hut. Watching big fish pass beneath your feet is the highlight of this circuit.

At feeding time you throw in pellets and small fish. Guides say large carnivorous fish such as groupers and trevally eat only small fish. Food is sold at a shop near the entrance, so confirm the price and amount locally.

Large fish such as the Napoleon wrasse (called mameng in the Philippines), the brown marbled grouper (lapu-lapu) and trevally (talakitok) are reported. Some are said to have grown for about ten years undisturbed to their maximum size. Some are protected species, so do not touch or catch them.

You can also see a rescued sea turtle, giant sea cucumbers, giant clams and lobsters. The owner explains that he does not keep these animals to eat or sell. One guide also writes that an injured dolphin was once nursed back to health and released.

Reviews say the water is so clear that you can see the fish well even without a mask. In some areas you can snorkel or swim in shallow water in batches of a set number of people. Wash off sunscreen completely before entering.

blocks.title: Combined with the Matnog island tour

children.text: A common plan covers Juag Lagoon, Subic Beach on Calintaan Island and Tikling Island on one boat charter. Subic Beach is on Calintaan Island and is described as having pale caramel sand, thatched cottages, a clean toilet and talisay trees for shade. Tikling Island is striking for its pinkish sand but is said to have almost no facilities. See the separate entry for Subic Beach.

In place of an entrance fee, donations are encouraged, and guides say you may also donate spare marine gear such as snorkels, goggles and fins. Souvenirs and lobsters sold on site help fund the operation.

children.text: Register your boat and the environmental fee at the Matnog tourism office and receive a safety briefing.
Reach Juag Lagoon by outrigger from the port. It takes about 20 minutes.
Cross the pens by raft, feed the fish and look around.
Move on to Subic Beach for swimming and lunch.
Stop at Tikling Island, then return to Matnog Port.
A guide says one boat takes up to 10 people, so gathering a group and splitting the fare reduces the burden.
On the first day, take the Matnog island tour to Juag Lagoon and Subic Beach.
Have dinner in Matnog town and rest at your lodging.
On day two, visit Bulusan Lake and the volcano area.
Matnog Port is where the ferries to Samar run, so it can be crowded early in the morning.

See also the Sorsogon City entry.
Register first at the Matnog tourism office and use an official boat. There is a warning that unofficial boats may lack life vests.
From the port to Juag is about
20 minutes
by motorized outrigger, and it can rock when the sea is rough.

One source says the sea is calm in the dry months of March–May. In the rainy season and typhoon season the waves off Matnog get rough, and some days boats do not run. Keep in mind too that currents are strong near the San Bernardino Strait.
During the day the sea is often calmer in the morning. Leaving early and returning before lunch is a sensible plan.

Near Matnog Port there are small lodgings and restaurants, and Sorsogon City (about an hour away) has more choices. Check prices and vacancies on a booking site. If your island plans start early, it is easier to stay a night in Matnog or a neighboring town.

At Subic Beach, reviews say you can have lunch of grilled sweetlips, grilled squid, fried scallops, chopsuey and coconut water. At the Juag hut, lobsters raised by the lagoon's owner and souvenirs are said to be sold. There is almost no food on the islands, so bring plenty of drinking water.

A Matnog itinerary is short, which suits touring the islands in the morning and moving on in the afternoon. If you are crossing to Samar, check ferry times first at the port office, and if you are heading to Bulusan Lake or Sorsogon City, check the last departure. Buying water and snacks at a shop near the port makes the islands easier.
Either wash off sunscreen completely before entering the water or do not apply it. It is prohibited here.
Use an official boat and the registration process at the Matnog tourism office. Check the life vests.
Bring cash. Cards are not accepted on the islands.
Do not grab or touch the fish. Some are protected species.
You can bring spare snorkels, goggles or fins to donate.
Boats rock, so bring motion-sickness medicine and a waterproof bag.
Keep noise down and do not startle the fish.
One tour report said a local tourism guide who comes along makes the explanations richer. If you want a guide, ask the tourism office.
Boats may not run depending on sea weather. Wear a life jacket and use only official boats.
Sunscreen is prohibited because it is said to harm the fish. If you break the rule you may not be allowed in the water.
Diving is prohibited. Snorkel only in the permitted area.
The waters off Matnog have currents and can be rough, so follow safety instructions.
The structures are bamboo and may be worn, so do not crowd too many people onto the raft and walkway at once.
Fees and rules can change from year to year, so check just before you go.
